blocks.text: About Ryan Beck — forecaster, sometimes writer, former bridge engineer.

blocks.label: The short version — body paragraph
blocks.text: I think about forecasting for a living, I've previously written some science fiction, and I have a history of getting sucked into all kinds of different hobbies.

blocks.label: The short version — body paragraph
blocks.text: I'm Director of Forecasting at Metaculus, where I wound up after becoming obsessed with forecasting and doing pretty good at it. Before that I worked as a bridge engineer for six years, and got a master's degree in civil engineering from Iowa State University.

blocks.label: The short version — body paragraph
blocks.text: I love sci-fi and fantasy, and wrote my own sci-fi novel, SEER, when I had an idea I was really excited about and wanted to try my hand at writing a book. I live in Iowa with my wife and three kids.

blocks.label: Education — body paragraph
blocks.text: I majored in civil engineering at Iowa State University, and got a master's degree in it as well. My master's thesis focused on the seismic behavior of hollow concrete columns. This involved designing a testing apparatus and scaled down hollow concrete columns and applying bending force until they broke, and measuring the strain in the reinforcement.

blocks.label: Education — body paragraph
blocks.text: It was an interesting project, I learned a ton, and I got to do a lot of design, coding, and analysis, which as you'll see are recurring projects I'm drawn to. But overall it was pretty grueling and I was glad to be finished with that.

blocks.label: Work — body paragraph
blocks.text: Currently I'm Director of Forecasting at Metaculus. Prior to getting into the forecasting world I did actually use my degree, spending a year working at LeMar Industries designing agricultural towers and catwalks, and then 6 years at HDR designing highway bridges. However, over time I became pretty bored with bridge engineering. It was hard to feel satisfied when you spend weeks documenting calculations on prespecified bridge geometry only to show that it works and maybe tweak a few rebar sizes up and down.

blocks.label: Work — body paragraph
blocks.text: During that time I found forecasting. I stumbled across an article about Superforecasters predicting the 2020 election, and that struck me as extremely satisfying.

blocks.label: Work — body paragraph
blocks.text: I'd always been interested in facts and evidence, and the idea of reducing bias in your opinions, sharing them as numeric probabilities, and seeing how accurate they wind up being sounded like an obvious extension of that that everyone should be doing. I made a few predictions on the 2020 election, and then forgot about them for a while until I got emails saying they'd been scored. I did pretty badly, but that motivated me to spend more time thinking about it, and I became a bit obsessed.

blocks.label: Work — body paragraph
blocks.text: That obsession led me to Metaculus where I began climbing the leaderboards, and briefly became a Pro Forecaster before I made the (frightening) leap of joining the Metaculus team full time in 2022, first as Forecasting Program Coordinator and in 2026 as Director of Forecasting. Since joining I spend less time making forecasts and more time designing forecasting projects, identifying the best forecasting questions to support decision-making, and managing the Programs team.

blocks.label: Hobbies — body paragraph
blocks.text: I have a bunch of hobbies that vary in intensity over time. Some are more persistent and have stuck around forever, such as reading (sci-fi, fantasy, and thrillers especially), board games, forecasting, visiting national parks, hiking, camping, video games, Magic the Gathering, and 3D printing. Others come in waves where I'm obsessed with them for a while until either the idea works its way out of my head or I burn out. These are some of the things you'll see on this site, like writing and coding projects, and other things like video editing.

blocks.label: Hobbies — body paragraph
blocks.text: Most of the second category of things are what you'll see on the projects page. Part of the motivation to revamp my website was making a place to share and document these things. Originally most of my coding projects were manual efforts that were partly for the end product and partly to learn to code, but these days I've transitioned more to <strike>yelling</strike> gently guiding AIs into producing what I want. So AI has taken a pass through my old coding projects and patched up the broken and outdated ones and given them some nicer polish, and has also lowered the barrier and time requirement for me to get ideas I think could be interesting or useful out of my head and into a tangible form.

blocks.label: Writing — body paragraph
blocks.text: Writing is a hobby that I've spent a big chunk of my life on, for fiction as a roughly two-year burst, while non-fiction / blogging has been a more persistent thing.

blocks.label: Writing — body paragraph
blocks.text: With blogging I've typically been drawn toward explainers, usually motivated by frustration over a perceived lack of depth in the conversation or me trying to get a better grasp on a topic. I love to write these kinds of things to clarify my own thinking, share what I've spent so much time getting up to speed on with others so it's easier for them and isn't all wasted on just me only, and to persuade and lay things out in what I consider to be a logical form. I tend to write mostly about politics, science, economics, and random things I've learned about.

blocks.label: Writing — body paragraph
blocks.text: Formerly these things were in the form of posts on Facebook and Google Plus that no one would read, then I made a home for them with my old website so no one could read them in a more organized fashion, and now infrequently on Substack at The Missing Nuance, so that no one can read them at a place made for hosting tons of things no one reads and a few things that lots of people do.

blocks.label: Writing — body paragraph
blocks.text: My fiction writing consisted mainly of two ideas that I had become very attached to and frantically needed to get out of my head. My short story, Not Human, was written as I was thinking about what humans are made up of and how much we could lose before we'd be noticeably different. And SEER is a novel that was motivated by thinking about free will, the age of data collection, artificial intelligence, autonomous drones, and predicting the behavior of individuals. I published it back in 2019 after working on it for a few years, and it's interesting (to me at least) to see what seemed prescient and not so prescient about it now that we're in the era of advanced LLMs.

blocks.label: Family — body paragraph
blocks.text: I live in Council Bluffs, Iowa, with my wife and three kids. Most of my free time is spent playing with them, taking walks, going on bike rides, hiking, going to sports and activities, camping, visiting national parks every year or two (mainly Grand Teton National park and sometimes Rocky Mountain National park), and all kinds of other things.

blocks.text: Printable family activity guides for national parks, by Ryan Beck.

blocks.label: National park guides — intro paragraph
blocks.text: A few years ago I got tired of having to research from scratch what there is to do at a couple of my favorite national park spots each time we went. So I made a couple quick reference guides with the relevant info. Because I have small kids, these are oriented around lighter hikes and family activities, so day hikes aren't on these. Be warned that they may be a bit out of date, but I expect they're mostly still accurate and at the least they'll be a great starting point for what options are available.

blocks.label: Section heading
blocks.text: Rocky Mountain National Park & Estes Park

blocks.label: Rocky Mountain National Park & Estes Park — small caption
Rocky Mountain National Park & Estes Park — body paragraph
blocks.text: RMNP requires day passes reserved in advance for different sections in the park. It can be tricky to get the passes and there are other cool things to do in the area, like in Estes, so this guide gives a number of options.

blocks.label: Grand Teton & Yellowstone — body paragraph
blocks.text: The big thing to know is if you want a camping spot you'll need to reserve it when they become available 6 months in advance (more for cabins). Otherwise this covers activities and hikes in the Tetons, and a day trip up to Yellowstone.

blocks.label: Projects — intro paragraph

blocks.label: Data Dashboards — body paragraph
blocks.text: Most of these were initially created to help with forecasting, but they tend to be genuinely interesting and useful data sources that were in need of nice visuals. Up to date (where possible) dashboards on the debt limit, refugee admissions, respiratory disease trends, semiconductor trade, the bird-flu cull, and more.

blocks.label: Herder — body paragraph
blocks.text: An app for herding a group toward a plan: propose activities, vote on them (ranked-choice if you like) and schedule around everyone's availability. Share a link; nobody needs an account.

blocks.label: March Madness 2026 — body paragraph
blocks.text: Making a bracket is fun, but if you're like me and know absolutely nothing about the teams involved or their general stats, this is for you. A bracket builder with relevant season stats, head to head histories, and some (shaky at best) power ratings all in one place.

blocks.label: National Park Guides — body paragraph
blocks.text: I love visiting Grand Teton National Park and Rocky Mountain national park, and wanted a reusable activity planning aid for families with small kids so I didn't have to recall anew each time what options there are. Short hikes, parking strategy, drive times, and more details.

blocks.label: Search + social description
blocks.text: Science fiction by Ryan Beck — SEER and Not Human.

blocks.label: Fiction — intro paragraph
blocks.text: I haven't written fiction for a while, but for a few years was very motivated by writing SEER and my short story Not Human. Learn more about them and how to check them out below.

blocks.label: SEER — body paragraph
blocks.text: The future is data. All Maria has to do is think about a simple task, like turning on the lights, and it happens. It's not magic, it's SEER, the government-operated algorithm that makes life in the 22nd century so idyllic. By harvesting massive amounts of personal data, SEER can predict what a person will want the moment they want it.

blocks.label: SEER — body paragraph
blocks.text: It's only when she's kidnapped by a group of anti-SEER rebels that Maria learns there's more to the algorithm than she knew. SEER is not just making people's lives easier; it's being used by those in power to control the public and stamp out potential opposition. At least, that's what Vincent, the leader of the rebel group, tells her.

blocks.label: SEER — body paragraph
blocks.text: Vincent needs Maria's cybersecurity expertise to take SEER down. But can she trust him? Bringing down SEER could free the country from its oppressive control — or it could be an act of horrific domestic terrorism, plunging the country into chaos. Either way, associating with the rebels has already made her the target of an army of autonomous combat drones. An army that can predict what she'll do before the thought even crosses her mind.

blocks.label: Not Human — body paragraph
blocks.text: What makes you human? As the first person in the world to have her mind copied to a machine, Lisa may soon learn the answer. Her copy's mechanical body is stronger and more durable than bone, flesh, and blood could ever be. But the dream of roboticists and neuroscientists everywhere may turn out to be a nightmare.

blocks.label: US debt limit — chart explanation
blocks.text: Shaded bands are the eight suspensions. The ceiling line breaks inside each one because there is no ceiling to plot; hovering a suspended date reads “no data” rather than zero. The trend is a least-squares fit to the run since the most recent change in the ceiling — a raise, or a suspension starting or ending — projected to the date that pace would reach the current ceiling. It is solid over the stretch it was fitted to and dashed beyond the last observation. During a suspension there is nothing to reach, so it runs a year out instead. It disappears when debt is already at the ceiling, as through the first half of 2025, when a projection would imply room that does not exist. Turn it off to fit the chart back to the data.

blocks.label: US refugee admissions by month — chart explanation
blocks.text: People admitted to the United States as refugees each month, from the State Department's Refugee Processing Center. Fiscal years run October to September; the annual ceiling is set by presidential determination and is a cap, not a target.

blocks.label: Refugee admissions by fiscal year — chart explanation
blocks.text: The same arrivals totaled by fiscal year. The dashed line is the annual ceiling, which is only published for recent years.

blocks.label: Big-tech revenue by fiscal year — chart explanation
blocks.text: Each company's full fiscal year, and the five added together. The combined line is blank for a year any of them has not finished reporting.

blocks.label: Big-tech revenue by quarter — chart explanation
blocks.text:
The same five by quarter, which is where the seasonality lives — Amazon and Apple both spike every December.

Two notes on the derivation. Quarters are selected by the length of the reporting period rather than by filing type, because a 10-K carries both the twelve-month total and three-month figures, and mixing them puts an annual number in the quarterly line. The fourth quarter is calculated as the annual total minus the three reported quarters, since a 10-K frequently reports the year without ever stating Q4 on its own.

blocks.label: US respiratory hospital admissions, weekly — chart explanation
blocks.text: New hospital admissions each week with a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis. Influenza and RSV are reported in the same returns. The shaded stretch is not a drop in admissions. Reporting to NHSN was mandatory under the public health emergency, became voluntary on 1 May 2024, and was made mandatory again by CMS on 1 November 2024. Hospital participation followed exactly: about 93% either side, and a low of 31% in October 2024. Counts inside that window are drawn from roughly a third of the hospitals, so they are not comparable with the rest of the line. The share reporting each week is in the download. A different series for the same measure, from the archived reichlab forecast hub, was widely used up to April 2024 and runs about 4% lower at the median. Figures read off older charts will not match these; that series is in the download for comparison.

blocks.label: US influenza hospitalizations — chart explanation
blocks.text: Weekly hospital admissions with a confirmed influenza diagnosis, from the CDC's FluSight forecasting hub. Per-state figures are in the companion file.

blocks.label: Influenza admissions, state by state — chart explanation
blocks.text:
Influenza admissions state by state, laid out roughly as the map is, so a bad week across one region reads as a block of color. It opens on percentage change against four weeks earlier, which is what makes a small state climbing fast as visible as a large one; the buttons switch to admissions per 100,000 over a window.

Every panel shares one vertical scale. Per head rather than raw counts is what makes that readable — on raw admissions the spread between the largest and smallest states is more than fiftyfold, and most of the grid flattens into slivers.

These come from the CDC’s FluSight hub, which republishes NHSN’s figures. They will not match the influenza line above to the digit: FluSight snapshots NHSN and does not always carry its later revisions, so recent weeks can differ by a few percent.

blocks.label: US semiconductor exports to China — chart explanation
blocks.text: Six-month rolling averages. The monthly lines behind them are in the legend, switched off to start with. The download also carries a twelve-month rolling sum.

blocks.label: China's semiconductor imports — chart explanation
blocks.text: Annual, and reported by China rather than by its trading partners, so this is the whole of what China buys from the world in the same two categories the chart above tracks for the US alone.

blocks.label: Chart title
blocks.text: Birds killed in the bird-flu outbreak

blocks.label: Birds killed in the bird-flu outbreak — chart explanation
blocks.text: Weekly count on the right-hand axis, running total on the left. They differ by two orders of magnitude, so on a shared scale the weeks would be a flat line along the bottom. The download splits each week into commercial and backyard birds, and carries the state, county and production type of every confirmed flock.

blocks.label: Chart title
blocks.text: COVID and flu patients in the hospital

blocks.label: COVID and flu patients in the hospital — chart explanation
blocks.text: Patients in the hospital on a given day, summed across reporting states, from the HHS hospital-capacity dataset. This is a census rather than a count of admissions — everyone in a bed that day, however long they have been there — so it runs far higher than the admissions series above and should not be read against it. HHS ended the reporting requirement behind it, so the series stops in April 2024.

blocks.label: Virginia COVID vaccinations — chart explanation
blocks.text: Counts rather than percentages, from the state’s open-data platform. The companion file carries the same figures split by age group.

blocks.label: Respiratory illness — page introduction
blocks.text: Weekly hospital admissions for COVID-19, influenza and RSV, nationally and state by state. National figures come from the CDC’s National Healthcare Safety Network. This is meant to be a census rather than a sample — CMS requires every acute care and critical access hospital to report weekly — but the requirement has lapsed once, and participation moves with it. Around 93% of hospitals report in a normal week, and the share behind each week is in the download. State-level influenza comes from the CDC’s FluSight forecasting hub. All of these count laboratory-confirmed admissions rather than everyone admitted with the illness, so they undercount by a margin that moves with how much testing is being done. They read more reliably as a trend than as a total.

blocks.label: The US debt limit — sidebar label
The US debt limit — page kicker
The US debt limit — page introduction
blocks.text:
Federal debt subject to the statutory ceiling, against the ceiling itself, from Treasury’s Daily Treasury Statement. Millions of dollars, updated each business day.

The shaded stretches are the eight occasions Congress has suspended the limit rather than raised it. There is no ceiling during a suspension, so the line stops rather than running flat — Treasury publishes a zero in that field, and plotting it would send the ceiling to the floor. When a suspension ends, the limit is reset to whatever the debt has reached by then.

blocks.label: Big-tech revenue — page introduction
blocks.text: Revenue for Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta and Microsoft, read out of their SEC filings, annually and by quarter. Billions of US dollars. The five do not share a fiscal calendar — Apple’s year ends in September and Microsoft’s in June — so the combined line is blank for any period where they have not all filed yet. Quarters are placed in the calendar quarter they end in, which is what lets the five line up; the consequence is that adding four calendar quarters for Apple or Microsoft will not equal their fiscal year.

blocks.label: US refugee admissions — page introduction
blocks.text:
People admitted to the United States as refugees, from the State Department’s Refugee Processing Center. Fiscal years run October to September, so the monthly series maps October through December onto the previous calendar year.

The annual ceiling is set by presidential determination and is a cap rather than a target: admissions have come in well under it far more often than they have approached it. The long view reaches back to 1975 — the two peaks are the Indochinese resettlement after the fall of Saigon and the Soviet and Southeast Asian programs around 1990.

blocks.label: Semiconductor trade — page introduction
blocks.text:
US exports of chips and chipmaking equipment to China, and what China buys from the whole world, from UN Comtrade. Values are US dollars.

Chips are HS 8542. Equipment is HS 8486, 903082, 903141, 854311 and 901041, summed. Monthly trade is noisy enough that the raw line is hard to read a trend off, so a six-month rolling average is carried alongside it.

The two charts are measured independently and will not reconcile. US exports are monthly and reported by the United States; China’s imports are annual and reported by China. Trading partners routinely disagree about the same shipments, since they classify goods differently and record them at different moments.

blocks.label: Bird flu — page introduction
blocks.text:
Birds killed in confirmed commercial and backyard flocks during the H5N1 outbreak, from USDA APHIS detection records.

A flock is counted on the date its infection was confirmed, and confirmation means the entire flock is depopulated — so a single commercial layer operation can add several million birds in one week. That makes the weekly figure extremely spiky and the running total the more readable line.

Backyard flocks are a large share of the detections and a very small share of the birds.

blocks.label: Virginia COVID — page introduction
blocks.text: People in Virginia by vaccination status, from the Virginia Department of Health. March 2021 to September 2023, when VDH stopped publishing; the history is complete for that window — nearly ten million rows, by locality, age group and vaccination status. Two days are wrong at the source. On 21 February 2023 VDH published every row two and three times over, which is collapsed here by taking one value per locality, age band and status. On 24 July 2021 the values themselves are exactly doubled with no duplicate rows to collapse, so that day is left blank and the line breaks there. For an age-stratified Virginia series, the HHS hospitalization panel on the respiratory page carries admissions broken down by age band from 2020 to 2023.
